title: John Turturro Says ‘I Still Consider Myself a Beginner’ as He Gets Marrakech Film Festival Tribute Award: ‘Every Job Is Like a First Love’
description:
Though his career has spanned over four decades, John Turturro still feels like it’s just the beginning.

	The 69-year-old actor and filmmaker was
body:
Though his career has spanned over four decades, John Turturro still feels like it’s just the beginning.

	The 69-year-old actor and filmmaker was honored with a tribute award at Marrakech Film Festival on Sunday night, where he was greeted with roaring applause as he mimed the iconic bowling moves of his “The Big Lebowski” character Jesus Quintana. He then gave a heartfelt speech about his work philosophy, which he said he got from his mom and dad.
	

	“I am a very fortunate person to make a good living as an actor, sometimes as a writer, a director, doing something that I deeply love. To put all of yourself into what you do and give a piece of that away in your work is something that I learned from my parents,” Turturro said. “They taught me that a job well done defines who you are. Building a house, making a dress was done brick by brick, stitch by stitch.”

	He called filmmaking the “magic and beauty of life” and “an offering that you hope others will receive with open hearts.”

	“A great writer, Cesare Pavese, once said that the only great thing in life is to begin. And I still consider myself a beginner in many ways,” he concluded. “For me, when I do a job, every job is like a first love. And I consider this award an encouragement to continue to try.”

	The award was presented to Turturro before a screening of his latest movie, “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” with director Noah Segan and producer Rian Johnson also on hand. The crime thriller stars Turturro as an aging pickpocket who steals a valuable USB drive from the heir to a crime family and must race to return it before the life of his disabled wife is threatened. Initially premiering at Sundance Film Festival earlier this year to praise from critics, the film was picked up by Sony Pictures Classics and released wide in U.S. theaters on Oct. 30.
	

	“As you get older, your toolbox of experience becomes fuller,” Turturro said of taking on the role. “You may not be able to jump as high or run as fast, but I absolutely think this is one profession that you can improve your product because you can learn to distill experiences … It was a gift to work on this film.”

	Turturro, a longtime champion of independent cinema, is perhaps best known for his collaborations with the Coen Brothers on four movies including “The Big Lebowski” and “Barton Fink,” and with Spike Lee on films including “Do the Right Thing” and “Jungle Fever.” He also starred in the “Transformers” film sereies and as supervillain Carmine Falcone in “The Batman” opposite Robert Pattinson. On the TV side, Turturro won an Emmy Award for his performance in comedy series “Monk” and currently stars in Apple TV’s acclaimed sci-fi thriller show “Severance.” 

	Turturro’s Marrakech Tribute Award follows that of Jeff Goldblum, who received the honor from his “The Grand Budapest Hotel” co-star Tilda Swinton. Other starry guests at the festival, whose jury is being led by Oscar winner Marion Cotillard, include Rian Johnson, Luca Guadagnino, James Gray, Monica Bellucci and more. 

	Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.

title: Huelva Ibero-American Film Festival Prizes: ‘After Elena,’ Alfredo Castro, Lucía Puenzo and ‘La Bola Negra’ Win Big
description: Spain’s Huelva Ibero-American Film Festival, one of Europe’s foremost Latin American cinema platforms, prized two of the region’s cinema greats, aw
body:
Spain’s Huelva Ibero-American Film Festival, one of Europe’s foremost Latin American cinema platforms, prized two of the region’s cinema greats, awarding top prizes to Chilean actor Alfredo Castro and Argentine writer-director Lucía Puenzo on Saturday night.

	“La Bola Negra” also reaped yet another plaudit, its scribe-helmer-producer duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi – Los Javis – scoring Best Spanish Direction.


	Huelva’s prizes highlight the festival’s focus under director Manuel H. Martín on crossover films, often mixing genre-bending and social issues to surprising effect. Top winner “After Elena.” from Chile’s Shawn Garry, turns on mourning but is a comedy; Lucía Puenzo’s “Pepita, the Gunslinger” is a gangster movie but the gangster is a woman who battles corruption. “Funk,” which won Duda Santos best actress, is a musical but “revolutionary,” says director Aly Muritiba, in its centering “Black joy.”
	

	The 2026 awards also may be the gayest in Huelva’s history, with nearly half going to LGBT movies in a year where Variety has asked whether the 2026-27 Oscars season is their gayest ever.

	The double nods for the Shawn Garry directed “After Elena”(“Después de Elena”) also underscore what Huelva does best: Highlighting titles that deserve further recognition which in the case of Latin America includes most of its movies, given they are under-covered by the international media.

	A TIFF world premiere sold by Meikincine and lead produced by Gabriela Sandoval out of her Cine Matriz label, “After Elena” is not just a study of grief but also a family dynamics comedy with the children of Roberto, 70, moving into his home to supposedly to look after him but also to get their hands on his wife and their mother Elena’s inheritance.
	

	Sluiced by a playful irony, “After Elena” took home Huelva’s Golden Columbus and Best Actor for Castro, once described by Variety as “reliably superb” though here acting against type, abandoning the “heightened performances I’m used to” for “strict, grounded realism,” he told Variety.

	Lucía Puenzo, the celebrated Argentine auteur (“XXY”) and pioneer of Latin American premium TV (“La Jauría,” “Señorita 89”) scored Best Director for “Pepita, the Gunslinger,” which reflects one of the things she does best: Wrapping gender-agenda issues in engrossing thriller narratives. Here Luisana Lopilato (“In Love and in Hate”) plays the real-life Margarita Di Tullio who rebelled against the deaths of fellow sex workers in 1980s Mar del Plata by founding her own brothel and nightlife business empire.

	“La Bola Negra’s” Best Spanish Direction Award in Huelva’s Acento Cine Español section marks the latest recognition from Los Javis’ native Spain, which scored the San Sebastián Festival Audience Award and has grossed a massive €40.4 million ($44.4 million) through Nov. 22, passing “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” to become the highest-grossing movie of any nationality in Spain his year, according to Rentrak Spain

	Allan Deberton’s “Gugu’s World,” Brazil’s crowdpleasing International Feature Oscar entry nabbed Huelva’s Audience Award, adding to other kudos such as a Berlin Generation Plus Crystal Bear and Guadalajara Maguey Best Film Award.

	Spain’s Rubén Ochandiano (“Broken Embraces”) scooped Best Supporting Actor for his performance as a musician who galvanizes the protagonist’s life in Mexican Lorena Villarreal’s “Life Is” (“La Vida Es”).

	Elsewhere, Huelva’s awards spotlighted disparate talents to track. Sharon Kleinberg’s “I Am Mario” walked off with Huelva’s Special Jury Prize. It turns on Mario, a forty-year-old trans taxi driver who faces an unexpected pregnancy which fulfils his dream to become a father but shatters some of his beliefs about masculinity. “I Am Mario” also won at Guadalajara Film Fest’s Maguey section , scooping its Jury Award in April.

	Best Actress was won by Brazil’s Duda Santos the skyrocketing star of telenovelas “Garota do Momento” and “A Nobreza do Amor” who plays in Aly Muritiba’s “Funk” a sassy, sexually frank funk singer MC Sabrina whose on-stage persona hides a fragility exposed during her pursuit of fame.
	

	Santos already shared with MC Nem a Tribeca 2026 Special Jury Mention for Best Performance in an International Feature. Huelva can now claim it was one of the first festivals in the world to recognise and prize Santos.

	Huelva Ibero-American Film Festival 2026 Awards

	Golden Colombus, Best Feature Film: “After Elena,” directed by Shawn Garr

	Special Jury Prize: “I am Mario,” directed by Sharon Kleiberg

	Best Director: Lucía Puenzo for “Pepita, the Gunslinger” (“Pepita, la pistolera”)

	Best Actor: Alfredo Castro, for “After Elena”

	Best Actress: Duda Santos, for “Funk”

	Best Supporting Actor: Rubén Ochandiano, for “Life Is”

	Best Spanish Direction: Javier Calvo, Javier Ambrossi for “La Bola Negra”

	Silver Columbus Audience Award: “Gugu’s World,” directed by Allan Deberton

	City of Huelva Honorary Award: Paulina García

	Silver Columbus, Best Andalusian Direction: Elías Pérez for “Plus Ultra”

title: Ina Garten Says She Turned Down ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Because the Thought of Competing Gave Her ‘Nightmares’
description:
Celebrity chef Ina Garten will not be cooking up a freestyle for “Dancing with the Stars” in the near future.

	Garten told Rose Byrne on a recent
body:
Celebrity chef Ina Garten will not be cooking up a freestyle for “Dancing with the Stars” in the near future.

	Garten told Rose Byrne on a recent episode of her “Happy Hour” podcast that she would be too nervous to compete. She opened the floor by asking Byrne if she had ever “not done something because it was too scary,” before answering her own question.

	“Somebody asked me to do ‘Dancing with the Stars,’” she said. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’” “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” Garten added.
	

	Garten may be shying away from the ballroom, but she is still dancing around the kitchen. Her Food Network show “Be My Guest with Ina Garten,” where she hosts guests at her house in East Hampton for food and conversation, entered its ninth season in October.

	While it wasn’t Garten, “Dancing with the Stars” still welcomed a celebrity chef this season. Giada De Laurentiis joined Season 35 with Alan Bersten as her partner. The couple competed two dances before being eliminated on Sept. 22 during “Viral Hits Night.”

	“Dancing with the Stars” will host its live finale on Tuesday on ABC and Disney+. The remaining competitors include podcaster and comedian Connor Wood partnered with Rylee Arnold, singer and actress Tatyana Ali partnered with Jan Ravnik, model Maura Higgins partnered with Mark Ballas, Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn partnered with Pasha Pashkov and Paralympic track star Ezra Frech partnered with Daniella Karagach.

title: ‘Hunger Games’ Lead Joseph Zada on Filming His Breakout Movie Role and ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’s’ Intense Stunts: ‘I Look Like a F—ing Action Star!’
description: When it comes to taking on the leading role in one of the most beloved film (and literary) franchises, sometimes you just have to jump right in. At
body:
When it comes to taking on the leading role in one of the most beloved film (and literary) franchises, sometimes you just have to jump right in. At least that was the case for Joseph Zada, whose first day on set of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” was spent filming the opening cornucopia scene where nearly 50 children are released to fight to the death.

	It’s quite the introduction for Zada, who stars as a young Haymitch Abernathy, the victor of the 50th Hunger Games and the future mentor to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson). (Woody Harrelson played Haymitch in the 2010s movies.) When Haymitch is selected for the Second Quarter Quell, the odds seem stacked against him. He should be celebrating his 16th birthday, but instead, he’s fated to enter the deadly arena as one of 48 tributes — double the usual number for Panem’s annual Hunger Games.
	

	There’s a certain amount of pressure that comes with stepping into such an iconic role, but Zada relished being thrown into the chaos. The first five weeks of filming were dedicated to shooting inside the arena — a “genius” scheduling choice, the 21-year-old actor tells Variety — because it let Zada fully immerse himself in the environment that would change Haymitch forever.

	“It was really good for stepping into the character’s body, and I started mainly working by myself and living in my character by myself before I had to go on and work with veterans in this crazy cast,” Zada says, referring to the film’s star-studded ensemble that includes Glenn Close, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons and Oscar winner Kieran Culkin. “I was able to just get on set and be confident and work with the younger actors first before I had to go into the bigger scenes and heavy dialogue.”
	

	Starting with such an intense sequence wasn’t an issue for Zada; he leaned into the movie’s intensity from the moment he auditioned, which occurred before Suzanne Collins’ novel was published. Zada was filming Netflix’s “East of Eden,” but he flew home to Australia to put together his tape. The instructions were simple enough: improvise a scene for a younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch. But Zada has never been one to take the easy route.

	Zada wrote four scenes that required using a drone and finding a stand-in for Maysilee, the character ultimately played by Mckenna Grace. He also enlisted help from his father and brother, who are also actors. The art of elevating an audition has become something of a family tradition for the Zadas, whether casting directors ask for it or not. (“They usually don’t,” Zada quips.) 

	“I didn’t go to acting school, but I have my own acting school at home with my older brother and my dad, where we did like four years of auditions,” he explains. “A standard audition is like propping yourself up against a white wall, and then just shooting and reading the scene, but we always just made a meal out of everything. We’d turn it into a little short film.”

	Zada had just two weeks to submit his audition tape, but, seeing as he was then focused on the Florence Pugh-led Netflix series and didn’t want to miss his chance to play Haymitch, he decided to take a risk. 

	“I had a two-week deadline, and then I just told them that they could have it in five weeks, because I had a whole plan for it,” he says, laughing. “Took that risk, and it paid off!”



	

					Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping”
									©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	Zada has been a fan of “The Hunger Games” for as long as he can remember, so joining the franchise was an opportunity he (clearly) didn’t take lightly. To prepare, Zada read Collins’ manuscript several times and, although he also studied Harrelson’s performance in the movies, he made a conscious effort to not focus too heavily on replicating his predecessor’s specific mannerisms.

	“I was just more worried about the voice, and then I think everything else was going to fall into place if I just played the truth of the scene,” Zada says. “The scenes are so beautiful, and I had the book to constantly refer to. I just trusted that it would all work out, and the fans would enjoy it.”
	

	Zada was also tasked with executing some of the film’s physically demanding action scenes. Between the combat, explosions and other deadly threats, there’s no shortage of danger surrounding Haymitch. One particular explosion sequence, which features a dramatic slow-motion shot, ultimately became Zada’s favorite moment to watch back.

	“It’s ridiculous!” he laughs. “I look like a fucking action star! It’s just not real. Like I’m watching it, and that is not me. There’s no way that I’m doing that right now. I look so cool!”

	Another particularly intense sequence was an underwater scene that Zada filmed on his final day of production. To prepare, Zada spent three weeks taking scuba lessons, training on the weekends while filming during the week. For the scene, he would descend underwater with an oxygen tank; then, when he heard “Action,” the crew would remove his air supply and activate the jets. It took some trial and error to determine how much force was needed to pull off the right look.

	“One time, they made the jets too heavy, and I flew off it and actually hit a pole,” he recalls. “They had to get someone to come down and give me air. Pretty scary!”

	Readers of Collins’ novel know that Haymitch experiences considerable trauma after the games, too, which plays out over the film’s final 30 minutes. Zada filmed at least one emotionally demanding scene a week and says it was “unavoidable” for the experience to take a toll on him as an actor.

	“Halfway through my week, I’d just be extremely depressed for an entire day,” he recalls. “It was really a lot.”

	Then, during reshoots, Zada had to revisit those taxing moments over nearly three consecutive days, sometimes shooting as many as 10 scenes in a single day. Even when a scene amounted to only a brief moment in a montage, the actor had to find his way back into the same devastated headspace.

	“I don’t understand actors that are able to switch in and out of it. I have to kind of stay in it for a while before [the scene] and, inevitably, after,” Zada says. “Right now, in my career, I’m not really scared of just going to those places a lot.”

	But even with the physical danger and emotional demands, the experience was well worth the risk for Zada, who hopes to approach every project with the same level of commitment.
	

	“I just want to throw myself completely in the deep end with every project,” Zada says. “It helps so much, so much having that in the arena, because that’s just my character the whole time. He’s really going for it, and I was like, ‘There’s no way for me to do this believably unless I’m throwing myself down that mountain or really pushing myself to the edge of death and injuring myself every day.’ There was no other way for me to do that and make it believable.”

	Not many people can understand what it’s like to star in an immensely popular book-to-screen adaptation like this, but Zada got to meet one of them at “The Hunger Games” prequel’s NYC premiere last Monday. Of course, Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson were there, but so was Walker Scobell, who plays the titular demigod in “Percy Jackson and the Olympians.” Fans quickly recognized the similarities between the two curly-haired protagonists fighting for a better world — not to mention that Season 3 of the Disney+ show shared a release date with the “Hunger Games” prequel.

	“I’m excited to see what Walker’s done with the new season,” Zada says about his Hollywood compatriot. “He’s a fantastic young actor, and I’m happy that we’re grouped together.”

schema.headline: ‘Hunger Games’ Lead Joseph Zada on Filming His Breakout Movie Role and ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’s’ Intense Stunts: ‘I Look Like a F—ing Action Star!’

title: Sheila Mangubat, ’90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days’ Star, Dies at 35
description:
Sheila Mangubat, who appeared on the reality series “90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days,” has died. She was 35.

	David Dangerfield, Mangubat’s form
body:
Sheila Mangubat, who appeared on the reality series “90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days,” has died. She was 35.

	David Dangerfield, Mangubat’s former fiancé, announced her death in an Instagram post shared on Saturday. A cause of death was not shared. 

	“It breaks my heart to share the news from her family that Sheila passed away on Saturday in the Philippines,” he wrote. “I am devastated and still trying to process this loss. Please keep her son, her family, and me in your prayers. Thank you for all your love and support.” 
	

	Dangerfield and Mangubat first connected in 2021 through a Facebook group for deaf singles, and dated long-distance (Dangerfield lived in Omaha, Neb. at the time, while Mangubat was born and raised in the Philippines). The two went on to get engaged, and their relationship was documented on the sixth season of TLC’s “90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days,” which aired in 2023. The couple split in Oct. 2025 following K-1 visa issues.

	“90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days” follows Americans who believe they’ve found their soulmate online, per TLC’s official description. They then travel abroad to meet them in person for the first time, navigating cultural differences while deciding whether or not to get engaged. “90 Day Fiancé” follows already engaged couples who must decide whether to ultimately get married or break up.

	Mangubat’s sister, Grace, also shared a tribute to the reality star, as was reported by People. “Rest in peace my beloved sister Shiela Mangubat… fly high my sister we will miss you,” she wrote in a Facebook post.
	

	Mangubat is survived by her son, Jhonreil.

schema.headline: Sheila Mangubat, ’90 Day Fiancé: Before the 90 Days’ Star, Dies at 35

title: Noah Schnapp Says He Auditioned to Play Haymitch in ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: ‘They Picked Right for This One’
description:
The odds were not in Noah Schnapp’s favor when it came to joining “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”

	The “Stranger Things” actor reveale
body:
The odds were not in Noah Schnapp’s favor when it came to joining “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”

	The “Stranger Things” actor revealed on social media on Saturday that he had auditioned for the lead role of Haymitch. “POV: my audition for Haymitch,” he wrote on his Instagram story. Tagging leading man Joseph Zada, Schnapp added, “Think they picked right for this one.”


	The prequel “Hunger Games” film follows Zada as Haymitch through his tumultuous experience during the 50th annual Hunger Games and the beginning of the revolution. The fifth installment of the franchise is based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel of the same name. It comes three years after the franchise’s first prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.” Zada is joined by a star-studded cast including McKenna Grace, Jesse Plemons, Kieran Culkin, Maya Hawke and more.
	

	Schnapp may be onto something with his casting assessment, given the prequel’s massive box-office success over opening weekend. The highly anticipated film opened to $120 million domestically and earned $105 million internationally for a global tally of $225 million.

	While he may have been denied the coveted role in “Sunrise on the Reaping,” Schnapp is still booked and busy. The 22-year-old actor is currently starring in Andy Sandberg’s play “Affluenza,” marking his professional stage debut at Riverside Studios in London. The dark comedy, inspired by real-life events, follows 16-year-old Dylan (Schnapp) dealing with the aftermath of causing a fatal drunk-driving crash in the Hamptons. Alongside Schnapp, the cast includes Janette Manrara, Juliet Cowan, Wallis Currie-Wood and Rupert Young.

title: Jeff Goldblum, Marion Cotillard and John Turturro Dine With Morocco’s HRH Prince Moulay Rachid at Starry Royal Gala During Marrakech Film Festival
description: Jeff Goldblum, Marion Cotillard, John Turturro and more stars got the royal treatment on Saturday night at a glitzy dinner hosted by Morocco’s His
body:
Jeff Goldblum, Marion Cotillard, John Turturro and more stars got the royal treatment on Saturday night at a glitzy dinner hosted by Morocco’s His Royal Highness Prince Moulay Rachid and Her Royal Highness Princess Lalla Oum Keltoum during the Marrakech Film Festival.

	Held at the 16th-century El Badi Palace — known for its stunning architecture and dramatic ruins — guests were greeted with fresh passion fruit and strawberry juice (and by the palace’s resident orange tabby cat) before being ushered into the glass-walled hall for dinner.
	

	Raised above dozens of meticulously-set tables was a large head table, decorated with a smattering of colorful flowers, where the guests of honor took their seats. The entire room rose to its feet as HRH Prince Moulay Rachid and HRH Princess Lalla Oum Keltoum arrived, joining Marrakech Film Festival jury president Cotillard as well as Goldblum and Turturro, who are both receiving career tributes. The festival was created by HRH Prince Moulay Rachid’s brother Mohammed VI, the King of Morocco, 23 years ago, with the entire royal family still heavily involved in the black-tie affair.

	Other guests seated at the head table included Cotillard’s fellow jury members Emma Mackey, Vicky Krieps, Claes Bang, Gilles Lellouche, Kaouther Ben Hania, Andrew Haigh, Ramata-Toulaye Sy and Saïd Hamich Benlarbi, as well as festival director Melita Toscan du Plantier. There were plenty of bold-faced industry names seated throughout the room, including Francesca Scorsese, daughter of director Martin Scorsese, who is a friend of the festival, and Mubi CEO Efe Cakarel.
	

	While a live orchestra played famed scores from throughout cinema history, attendees were served a traditional Moroccan feast including lamb tagine, a mound of couscous and pastillas, which was, of course, accompanied by plenty of mint tea.

	As the dinner wound down, guests got up out of their seats to mingle and migrate to a more intimate room. Red velvet couches invited guests to settle in, while photos of famous faces who had graced the festival throughout years past dotted the walls. Goldblum and his wife, Emilie Goldblum, chatted animatedly to Mackey while Krieps — who was sporting a chic headscarf printed with red roses — caught up with Cakarel.

	The Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28, when Cotillard and her jury will award one of the 14 competition films — consisting of first and second features — the prestigious Étoile d’Or.

schema.headline: Jeff Goldblum, Marion Cotillard and John Turturro Dine With Morocco’s HRH Prince Moulay Rachid at Starry Royal Gala During Marrakech Film Festival

title: Rian Johnson Cites Curry Barker as Reason to Be Optimistic About Future of Indie Filmmaking: ‘Youtube Is Just What Sundance Was in the ’80s’
description:
Rian Johnson is hopeful about the future of indie filmmaking.

	During a converation at Marrakech Film Festival on Sunday afternoon, the “Star Wars
body:
Rian Johnson is hopeful about the future of indie filmmaking.

	During a converation at Marrakech Film Festival on Sunday afternoon, the “Star Wars: Last Jedi” and “Knives Out” director specifically cited Youtube as one of the most effective ways for early-career filmmakers to get their movies discovered.

	Johnson reflected on a recent conversation he had with 27-year-old director Curry Barker, who was discovered on Youtube before catapulting to fame with his box-office breakout “Obsession.” “YouTube to me isn’t a new form or some new scary paradigm,” Johnson said. “YouTube is just what Sundance was in the ’80s. It’s a way to get your movie out there so that people can see it.”
	

	Johnson acknowledged that traditional film festivals still play an important role in launching indie filmmakers’ careers, but argued that online platforms have opened up opportunities that didn’t exist for previous generations.

	“Even though there are a lot of things that are really hard right now about starting out as a filmmaker, that’s one of the exciting things,” he continued. “Besides festivals, there are also other ways to build audiences, by making shorts and getting them out there and people discovering them. And there’s a million different ways to get your feature out there.”

	Barker’s career is a particularly compelling case study. The filmmaker first built an online following alongside comedy partner Cooper Tomlinson through their YouTube channel “that’s a bad idea,” before pivoting into horror with the 2023 short “The Chair,” which amassed millions of views. His next project, the found-footage horror film “Milk & Serial,” was made for just $800 and released for free on YouTube in 2024, where it became a viral sensation.
	

	The film’s success attracted Hollywood’s attention, leading Barker to sign with UTA in 2025 and eventually make the leap to theatrical filmmaking with “Obsession.” The supernatural horror film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, where it sparked a bidding war before landing distribution with Focus Features. Released theatrically in May 2026, the microbudget production became a breakout box-office success.

	Filmmakers including Kane Parsons, whose viral “Backrooms” videos led to an A24 feature, have similarly turned Youtube followings into Hollywood opportunities.

	Johnson, meanwhile, has firsthand experience with the traditional festival pipeline. His 2005 feature debut, “Brick,” starring Joseph Gordon-Levitt, premiered at Sundance, where it won a special jury prize.

	“There’s something really special about watching someone’s first feature,” Johnson said, praising Marrakech’s commitment to showcasing debut and sophomore features. “You know they have been cooking it and its been building in their mind and they’ve been thinking about it, so in some ways there’s nothing more expressive or purer than seeing a first feature from someone.”

	He reflected on how challenging it was to find a wide audience for “Brick,” which he began writing when he was 22. “I spent my 20s trying to get it made and failing and I finally made it when I turned 30,” he said. “So it took me eight years to get it made. And all this time the idea was baking and stewing in my head.”

	Their shoestring budget only allowed them 19 days to shoot the entirety of the film, but Johnson said: “I think anyone who’s making a movie on that tight a schedule knows the only way to do it is by prepping and knowing what you’re doing when you get in there.”

	“And you just do it because you have to do it,” he continued. “I don’t know if the less resources felt like less resources, it just felt like this is the way we’re making this particular movie.”

	Still, Johnson argued that the platform itself matters less than the work filmmakers are putting into the world.

	“If you make something that connects with people, and if you have something to say and you have something in your heart, and you’ve practiced your craft so you can do it effectively, that’s still an incredibly rare thing and something that everybody is looking for,” he said.
	

	“Whether it gets into a festival or whether people start discovering you online or whatever, there’s so many things that make it hard,” Johnson continued. “But I truly believe that is the gold coin that everybody is searching for in the world. So the more opportunities you have in the world to do that and get your work out there, the better, I think.”

	Johnson said that he has that personal connection with “Star Wars,” because he grew up with the franchise “almost as a religion.” Naturally, he jumped at the chance to direct 2017’s “The Last Jedi,” which he said is still “the most joyful process of any movie I’ve ever made.”

	“I felt just so connected to it, and just cared so deeply about every single element of it,” Johnson continued. “I think especially with something that has a big cultural impact and belongs to everybody, that makes it even more important for you and the entire team to make it personal for yourselves, to make sure it’s coming from a personal perspective and something that’s deeply on fire inside of you.”

	As for if he would ever return to the franchise — Johnson was previously attached to write a new “Star Wars” film trilogy, but the project was eventually scrapped — never say never. 

	“I love ‘Star Wars’ more now than I ever have. And it’s exciting to me that there are a lot of different voices now, taking cracks at it,” he said. “I’m already writing the next thing I’m gonna do, and it’s not a ‘Star Wars’ thing or a ‘Knives Out’ thing. Right now, I’m very much enjoying making my own stuff, but if the opportunity presented itself, it’s a world I deeply love.”

title: Noah Kahan Deserved a Lot More Grammy Love Than Just One Minor Nomination. Here’s Why He Didn’t Get It
description: In previous eras of less pervasive social media, we usually could only guess at just how disappointed music and film personalities were when they
body:
In previous eras of less pervasive social media, we usually could only guess at just how disappointed music and film personalities were when they didn’t fare well with Grammy or Oscar nominations. But lately, more and more major and minor figures have been up-front and honest in sharing with their fans that, hey, yes, they’re feeling the apparent lack of industry love, too. As long as these reflections come off as more bummed out and philosophical than bitterly entitled or peevish — here’s looking at you, John Summit — they can make for a moment of connection between artists and their fan base. And so it is that, this past week, I followed one of our most likably candid superstars through what I came to refer to as the Five Stages of Noah Kahan Grammy Grief. 

	Kahan himself skipped over the anger phase, though his fans certainly felt that one, when it turned out that their hero got passed over for everything but one relatively modest nom, in defiance of all expectation. There were other stages they went through together. First came uneasy anticipation: The day before nominations came out, Kahan issued a whatever-will-be-will-be-type tweet, almost as if he’d gotten a hint that things were not going to go well for him. (“Whatever happens tomorrow I love you all and I have done everything I’ve ever needed to do in my career because of YOUR support.”) Then came resignation and premature acceptance: “Life goes on.” Then came gallows humor, as he took a fake phone call on stage from the Grammys and quipped, “Wrong number.” And finally, there was real acceptance, as he admitted in an affecting stage monologue that he was having a teachable moment as, without mentioning the awards, Kahan said he was assessing why he had hoped too much for something and put the value of his worth in the wrong place. 

	Undoubtedly, some would say he should have just put himself above it all and not even referenced the seeming snub, but my admiration is always going to go more toward people who address elephants in rooms. So maybe now he could move forward with his usual good humor… while, sure, having the fact that he just sold out his next 24 U.S. stadium shows to keep him warm at night.

	But maybe us Grammy prognosticators aren’t yet ready to move on, because like pollsters in 2024, we want to figure out how we got Kahan’s chances wrong. And really, he was the only significant thing we forecasted incorrectly, since virtually everything else in the top three categories went as predicted, for once. Kahan seemed to have almost everything going for him, being the only artist who consistently had not just one but two albums in the top 10 all year long, on top of having recently become one of the biggest ticket-sellers in the business… and, lest the predictions be based only on popular appeal, he’d also gotten mostly great reviews lately, although he hadn’t started out his career as a critical favorite.


	Professional prognosticators nearly all had Kahan’s “The Great Divide” album landing one of the eight open slots for album of the year, and most entertainment news outlets predicted the same for the title track in the fields of record and/or song of the year. The forecasters lining up to say he was close to a sure thing included those at Billboard, Rolling Stone, the Hollywood Reporter, Hits and, yes, Variety. Over at the awards site Gold Derby, “Great Divide” was seen as all but locked in for an album nomination no matter which of their columns you looked down — industry experts, their editors, or the site’s active followers. Instead, he wound up with a lone nod for… best contemporary folk recording, which was rather like the Recording Academy setting a bull down in a china shop instead of at the rodeo.


	There was one obvious stumbling block on the path to considering him a shoo-in for one of more big nods: the fact that he’d only gotten two nominations before, and only one as the primary person nominated. Kahan was nominated as best new artist for the 2024 Grammys (and lost to the empirically less popular Victoria Monet); his only other prior nom was in a country category as the featured duet partner on a Kelsea Ballerini single. But surely we were past the point now — we thought — where anyone still had to dude-splain Noah Kahan to the Grammy elite. 
	

	Of course it shouldn’t matter if “The Great Divide” spent most of 2026 in the top 10 hovering just above the continued presence of the four-year-old (!) “Stick Season.” if these albums blew chunks… which is the kind of thing that’s been known to sink a Grammy nomination. But “The Great Divide” demonstrably does not fall into the realm of suckage. If anything, it represents the kind of perfect storm the Grammys have traditionally loved to reward, where somehow, some way, songwriting that is idiosyncratic and qualitatively strong and unique captures the imagination of the masses who might usually be stereotyped as tending toward less distinctly personal fare. Kahan could have been seen as having it all…
	

	Except for having a natural constituency among Recording Academy members.

	Therein lies a rub. It did nag at me, even as I was making my own forecast that he’d get into the top categories, that I couldn’t picture in my mind’s eye which subset of voters would be putting their support behind him. In terms of either genre or geography, he did not and does not have the wind at his back.

	The Recording Academy has 12 chapters spread across the U.S. This may come as a shock, but none of them are in Burlington. There’s a Pacific Northwest chapter, but good luck looking for a corresponding Atlantic Northeast chapter. Surely Kahan would be the first to laugh at the idea of his New England industry homies colluding as a voting bloc to ensure vindication for Vermont.

	The genre thing looms as an even bigger problem. Leaving aside the general field at the top of the ballot, where does a Kahan rightfully belong among the 90+ stylistically divided categories that follow? You could consider him rock. Billboard certainly does; he has two songs in the top 10 of the rock airplay chart right now (“Orbiter” and “Draw You Out”). But are the voters who choose to vote in the rock categories — and as you probably know, they don’t get to vote in all 100 — really going there to vote for a guy like Kahan, as opposed to the harder stuff? He would seem like a closer fit for the Americana and American roots categories. But the Americana community hasn’t really fully embraced him, even though he has shown up to their events. He didn’t come up through their farm system, and in a genre that deliberately favors underdogs, he might’ve simply gotten too popular too fast. So, “contemporary folk recording” it is, even if that is one oddball catch-all category. (But as has been pointed out, there are people nominated in that every year who have the nom as a highlight of their professional careers, so there should be no shame in it for Kahan, and he’d undoubtedly agree.)
	

	If you really want to know why we all should have seen Kahan’s near-shutout coming, anyway, consider the ongoing case of Zach Bryan, who also falls between genres, despite also being one of the biggest recording and touring artists in the universe at the moment. I thought of Bryan as I was wondering whether Kahan would face the same problem with the Grammys, but at the time, I thought Bryan might have been snubbed most of all because of his surlier personality, whereas Kahan being an overtly personable guy would make the difference. Turns out they’re probably just in the same ballpark after all.

	And then there is the issue of white guys with guitars, and how they’re doing, generally, in the culture, or with the Grammys specifically. The demographics the Recording Academy has been courting in expanding and diversifying its membership do not suggest they’re bringing in vast amounts of people who are going to put a Kahan at the top of their ballot, any more than they’re going to vote for Paul McCartney (whose critically hailed “Boys of Dungeon Lane” would have been a shoo-in for top noms with the Grammy voters of the 2000s, but not the 2020s). When the Grammys invited 3,600 pros to join as voting members in the class of 2025, 56% were people of color and 60% were under 40. You don’t look at those stats and imagine that any of the various waning subgenres of rock are suddenly going to be overrepresented among the biggest Grammy nominees. 

	But here’s the other thing to take into account: all those new voters, along with the older ones the Academy has not aged it out, are getting it right more often than not. As much as I like “The Great Divide,” when I look at the album of the year lineup to see which nominee I would personally knock out to make room for it, there are only a couple of the eight that seem even remotely expendable. Most forecasters would probably say that Phoebe Bridgers’ “Lost Weekend” took a slot that was expected to go to Kahan, and maybe she knocked him down to ninth place, although we’ll never know for sure where he ended up. There’s absolutely nothing regrettable about her making it in, or the utterly deserving Rosalía or Raye or most of the others… and obviously no shame in women earning seven out of eight noms in some of the top categories, after the “step up, girls” era, and on merit. Of all the years for any sense of overriding Grammy outrage to take hold, this is not one of them.

	But I can think of other artists besides Kahan I think got “robbed” in the top categories, like Sienna Spiro, who should have been up for all four top general-field trophies but is only in for best new artist. A year this solid and action-packed makes the case that the Academy should considering reupping the number of finalists in the top four categories from eight to 10, as was the case in 2022 and 2023 before tjeu dropped it back down again. If the Oscars can stick with 10 nominees at the top of the ballot, so could the Grammys.

	In the meantime, as Kahan fans lick wounds, they ought to be able to take some comfort in the hundred factors that make even a worthy contender get shut out, or nearly ignored. It’s not him, it’s them — in all sorts of ways — and there are real reasons to believe that, not just the delusional ones hardcore stans come up with to justify more negligible artists being slighted. And if the reasons for being left out have to do with being the kind of artist who snuck up completely between the cracks, and who’s thriving beyond belief, even as he continues to be a little bit stepped over, that’s a triumph that might finally be even better than a Grammy.

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Becomes Rare Documentary to Surpass $100 Million Globally
description:
“You Can See Everything” has surpassed $100 million globally, a rare box office milestone for a documentary. 

	So far, the zeitgeist-capturing loo
body:
“You Can See Everything” has surpassed $100 million globally, a rare box office milestone for a documentary. 

	So far, the zeitgeist-capturing look at Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has generated a staggering $93.4 million at the domestic box office and $9 million overseas for a worldwide tally of $102.4 million. It continues to mint money for A24, which produced the film in secret for roughly $7 million.


	Over the weekend, “You Can See Everything” opened in the United Kingdom with $3.2 million from 596 locations. Those ticket sales register as A24’s second-largest debut in the territory behind “Backrooms” ($5.7 million). Similar to in the United States, around 70% of the audience in the U.K. was under 35 years old. Australia and New Zealand are currently the top-grossing markets with $3.8 million.
	

	Elsewhere, the film is getting a staggered rollout at the international box office: it’s also playing in Turkey, Poland, the Czech Republic, Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Greece (contributing around $2 million in total), and it’ll debut over the next few weeks in other territories including Mexico, Brazil and Argentina (Nov. 26 and 25), Germany, Austria and Hong Kong (Dec. 3 and 4), Spain (Dec. 25), France (Dec. 30) and Japan (March 12). A24 is handling the release in select territories, with Sony distributing in markets including Denmark, Norway, Sweden and the Middle East.

	Already, “You Can See Everything” is one of the biggest theatrical documentaries in years. It’ll rely on overseas audiences to topple the genre’s all-time record. Michael Moore’s seminal 2004 film “Fahrenheit 9/11” is the highest-grossing documentary in history with $222 million globally, including $119 million domestically and $103 million overseas; followed by “March of the Penguins” with $127 million globally, including $77 million domestically and $50 million overseas.
	

	Directed by comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim, “You Can See Everything” became a word-of-mouth smash after a surprise world premiere at Telluride Film Festival. The movie opened to $15 million domestically in mid-October and, with sensational reviews, remained a big-screen draw throughout the fall. The nearly three-hour-long doc takes place over three years and begins as Holmes, the founder of the health technology company Theranos, is preparing for her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.

              In the photo Tallulah shared yesterday ... Tallulah held hands with the "Die Hard" star on a porch swing.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              After taking the pic down ... Tallulah wrote that despite finding the moment she shared with her father "super sweet," she "didn't think farther ahead that this was possibly too intimate a photo to show."

And he's still always the absolute hero we know him to be."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              Tallulah also shared more about her visit with Bruce ... saying the two watched a video of Frankie Valli performing.
      
    
              As you know ... the Hollywood legend retired from the big screen after being diagnosed with aphasia and frontotemporal dementia.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Tallulah has defended her dad in the past ... calling out a report earlier this month that cited a source claiming he was acting like a baby.
      
    
              She wrote, “So the 'friend,' 'family member,' or source who shared that he 'acts like a baby now?' How is that acceptable? Who are you?"

              However, Natalie's story fell apart when authorities found zip ties and duct tape in her car, a Maserati ... according to investigators.
